Four Tools First
MADE WITH CLAUDE · LAB EDU · 00:00:42:23

Four tools.Then the video.

A 43-second reel about the four tools that turn Claude Code from a chatbot into an edit suite: Remotion renders the video, ElevenLabs gives it a voice with every word timed, Whisper writes the subtitles and FFmpeg exports the final file. Each tool gets a repo card with its live star count and a demo of its job, timed to the voice word by word, all drawn in code on an HTML canvas. This is the full workflow, with the install lines.

01 · The idea

A chatbot, until it isn't.

Claude Code can plan a video, but on its own it only answers in text. The reel makes that visible: the hook asks for a reel and gets a flat wall of text back, a CHATBOT tag slams on, and then four tool cards snap into four empty sockets and the same chat turns into an edit suite.

From there it is a list with one block per tool, each in its own colour. Every block opens on a repo card that types the tool's name and rolls its star count, then the tool acts out its job on the words that describe it. A small Claude Code tracker in the corner installs them one by one, 0/4 to 4/4, and the close shows one prompt becoming a finished reel. Catalina, the Lab's character, presents it from the corner.

02 · The four tools

What each one does.

What each tool does in our pipeline, how Claude uses it, and the install line. Star counts and descriptions as shown on GitHub on 20 Nov 2026; they change, so check them live.

TOOL 01remotion-dev/remotion · "Make videos programmatically with React" · 74,410 stars

Remotion

What it does in our pipeline
Turns code into real video. Every scene is a React component that receives the current frame number, and Remotion renders each frame and encodes the MP4. It is how a description in a chat becomes an actual file.
How Claude uses it
Claude writes the components (layout, timing, springs), renders single stills to check them, then renders the whole piece from the command line.
Install
npx create-video@latest
# then, inside the project
npx remotion studio     # live preview
npx remotion render     # render the video
Note
Needs Node.js (a current LTS). Remotion has its own license terms for companies; read them on remotion.dev before commercial use.
TOOL 02Voice API · not a GitHub repo

ElevenLabs

What it does in our pipeline
A natural voice for the narration, plus the timing of what is said. The text-to-speech request "with timestamps" returns the start and end of every character, which Claude groups into words.
How Claude uses it
Claude sends the script, saves the audio and a words.json with the start and end of every word, and every animation cue reads its time from a word instead of a guessed second.
Install
# 1. Create an account on elevenlabs.io
# 2. Copy your API key from your account settings
# 3. Put it in a .env file in the project:
ELEVENLABS_API_KEY=your_key_here
# optional official SDK
pip install elevenlabs
Note
Keep the key out of any shared folder or repository. On the free plan, credit the voice in your caption ("Voice: ElevenLabs").
TOOL 03openai/whisper · "Robust Speech Recognition" · 113,133 stars

Whisper

What it does in our pipeline
Speech to text that runs on your own computer. It listens to footage or narration and writes subtitles with timings.
How Claude uses it
Claude runs it on raw footage to get a transcript to cut from, writes .srt subtitles, and reads the final narration back to confirm every word on screen matches what is said.
Install
pip install -U openai-whisper
# example
whisper audio.mp3 --model small --language English --output_format srt
Note
Needs Python and FFmpeg on your PATH. The first run downloads the model you pick.
TOOL 04FFmpeg/FFmpeg · 67,667 stars

FFmpeg

What it does in our pipeline
The command-line Swiss army knife for video and audio: it cuts, joins, mixes, measures loudness and encodes the final file.
How Claude uses it
Claude writes the commands: trims and joins clips, lays the voice and sound under the picture, checks −14 LUFS and exports H.264 at a real bitrate for Instagram.
Install
# Windows
winget install --id Gyan.FFmpeg -e
# macOS
brew install ffmpeg
# Debian / Ubuntu
sudo apt install ffmpeg
# check
ffmpeg -version
Note
Official downloads and builds: ffmpeg.org/download.html.
03 · References

What Claude needed before the first prompt.

This is the Lab's own piece, so the brand is ours. We studied a list reel we liked for its structure, frame by frame, and rebuilt the look from scratch in our own card language. These are the ideas it leans on, in general terms.

Proof on screen

A list of tools is only convincing if each one looks real. A repo card with the actual owner, name, description and a star counter that rolls up to the live number gives every claim a receipt.

A progress you can feel

The install tracker in the corner turns a list into a story with an ending: four empty slots, a spinner on the one being described, a green check when its line ends, a glow at 4/4.

A colour per tool

Every block floods the whole frame with its own colour: navy, deep green, amber, black. The viewer feels the next tool before reading its name.

Props that break out

On stressed words, things leave their card: the Remotion wordmark over the card's edge, the live frame popping out of the film strip, a final.mp4 card jumping out of the terminal.

No logo files

Each tool gets a simple generic mark drawn in code, not its real logo. The names, repo cards and colours carry the recognition.

Palette

The Lab's colours carry the frame; each tool block adds its own flood so the list reads at a glance.

#F6F0E6 cream#D97757 clay#141A2E navy
04 · One-time setup

Before the prompt.

Step 01

Install Claude Code.

Follow the official guide at docs.claude.com (Claude Code overview) for your system, then open it inside an empty project folder.

Step 02

Node.js and Python.

Node runs Remotion and the headless browser that renders canvas frames; Python runs Whisper and the audio checks.

Step 03

The four tools.

Install them with the lines in section 02 and put your ElevenLabs key in a .env file. Then ask Claude to check each one is reachable (ffmpeg -version, whisper --help, a test render).

Note

How this reel was drawn.

This particular reel was drawn on an HTML canvas, rendered frame by frame in a headless browser and assembled with FFmpeg. Remotion is what we use when a piece is built as React components; the method on this page works with either.

05 · Claude session

One brief, then the checks.

Below is the master prompt you can paste, followed by the two quality-control messages: the stills review and the final render.

00:01 · master prompt · claude code
Make a 43-second vertical reel for The AI Editing Lab, 1080x1920 at 30 fps, all in English. Topic: the four tools to install before you make a single video with Claude Code. Keyword: TOOLS.

1. Script. Hook in under 2 seconds: "Don't make a single video with Claude Code until these four are installed." Then: without them it's a chatbot, with them it's your whole edit suite. One line per tool, in this order: Remotion (turns Claude's code into real video, frame by frame), ElevenLabs (a real voice with every word timed), Whisper (listens to your footage and writes the subtitles), FFmpeg (cuts, joins and exports the final file). For the GitHub tools, say the star count rounded ("over seventy thousand") and show the exact live count on screen; check every count on GitHub today, never guess one. Close with: "Four tools, one prompt, a finished reel. Comment TOOLS and I'll send you the setup."

2. Voice. ElevenLabs, voice "Jessica", natural speed (1.0). Save the start and end time of every word to words.json; every cue reads its time from a word, never from a guessed second.

3. Look. Everything drawn in code on an HTML canvas, no real logo files (draw a simple generic mark per tool). One shared kit: cards with thick black outlines and a hard offset shadow (no blur); a GitHub-style repo card that types "owner / repo", slides the description in and rolls the star counter like an odometer (for ElevenLabs, an API card with a key field instead of stars); a small Claude Code install tracker bottom-left that goes 0/4 to 4/4, one slot per tool, ticking green on the word that finishes each tool's line. Every block floods the full frame with its own colour, starting just before the cut: navy for Remotion, deep green for ElevenLabs, amber for Whisper, black for FFmpeg, cream for the hook and the close. Lab colours: clay #D97757, cream #F6F0E6, navy #141A2E.

4. Demos. Each tool acts out its job on its own words: code typing into film frames, spoken words dropping onto a voice track, a waveform turning into a subtitles file, a film strip being cut, joined and exported. On stressed words, props break out of their cards.

5. Layout. Every text and prop inside x 90-960 and y 250-1480, each block full at its cut. Keep the bottom-right corner empty for our presenter.

6. Build. Three builders in parallel sharing the kit: one does the frame, the hook and the CTA; the other two take two tools each. Sound effects only on real events, voice on top, mix to -14 LUFS, true peak at or below -1.5 dB.

7. Process. Show me a stills sheet and a motion and originality check before the final render, and wait for my approval.

What came back: the script, a block-by-block storyboard with every stressed word mapped to a change on screen, the ElevenLabs narration with 112 time-stamped words, a shared kit (thick-outline cards, the repo card, the install tracker, the colour floods) and three builders working in parallel: one on the frame, the hook and the CTA, two on the tools, two each, all reading the same word clock.

00:02 · stills before render · claude code
Before the final render, export a stills sheet: one frame every 1.5 seconds from frame 0, with a red outline for the safe zone (x 90-960, y 250-1480). Check every block for: motion density (something changes at least once a second and on every stressed word, including the long demo blocks), fill (is the block full at its cut?), card fit (does every text fit its card, or does anything overflow?), numbers (does each star count on screen match GitHub today, and does the voice say the rounded version?) and originality (is every prop drawn for this line, or is anything a generic placeholder? Does any block repeat a prop or structure from our earlier reels?). List everything you find, fix it all in one pass and show me the sheet again.

What came back: one repo description was too long for its card and ran past the edge, so the card learned to shrink the line and, if needed, wrap it into two balanced lines. Motion density passed but sat close to the bar in the longer demo blocks, so each got an extra change on its stressed words. The star counts were checked again on GitHub before the render.

00:03 · final render · claude code
Approved. Now composite our presenter Catalina on top from her real images: her two short image-to-video clips at the start and at the end, and full-body poses from her character sheet in between, each swapped in place with a short crossfade on a block change; she never slides in or out. Render 1080x1920 at 30 fps, H.264 at 14 Mbps CBR, the mix at -14 LUFS, and give me a stills strip of the final.

What came back: 42.8 seconds at 1080×1920 and 30 fps, H.264 at 14 Mbps, the voice mixed to −14 LUFS.

06 · What Claude built

Four blocks, one kit.

HOOK

Chatbot → edit suite

A Claude Code window types "make me a reel" over four dashed sockets. On "chatbot" the frame goes grey and the reply sags into a wall of text; on "edit suite" it floods clay, the four tool cards snap into the sockets with cables to the window and the reply becomes four coloured tracks with a playhead.

REMOTION

Code into frames

The repo card types itself and a big plate rolls the stars to 74,410. Then a code editor types JSX, three lines leave it as glowing pills and fill the frames of a film strip, a FRAME counter ticks at 30 fps and the live frame breaks out of the strip.

ELEVENLABS

Every word a brick

An API card (key, voice, with_timestamps toggle) wakes a studio speaker that spits each spoken word out as a brick, landing on a voice track at its real start time. On "lands" a clay ANIMATION block slams onto the "word" brick in the same frame.

WHISPER

It listens, it writes

The repo card rolls to 113,133. Then a talking-head footage card feeds sound particles into a big ear, a playhead scans the waveform, and a subtitles.srt file types itself line by line; its first line flies into the video as a burned-in caption.

FFMPEG

Cut, join, export

Scissors snip a strip of takes and the bad one falls away, the pieces lock together with a b-roll clip, a terminal types the commands, and a final.mp4 card pops out of it next to a quality meter that fills to MAX.

CTA

One prompt, a finished reel

The four cards slap down in a row, one prompt bar types "make me a reel" and folds into a playing 9:16 reel fed by cables from every card. Then TOOLS types into a big clay comment pill and a "setup sent" bubble springs up.

// the Claude Code install tracker: every state change sits on a word
const TL_TR = {
  born: wi(12),                                           // "installed." → 0/4 card pops
  act: [wi(26), wi(45), wi(63), wi(83)],                  // "first / second / third / last"
  done: [wi(43) + 0.05, wi(61) + 0.05, wi(78) + 0.05, wi(96) + 0.05],   // "frame." · "word." · "subtitles" · "quality."
  all: wi(102),                                           // "finished" → every slot glows
  out: wi(104) + 0.1,                                     // "Comment" → leaves, the CTA gets the stage
};
for (const d of TL_TR.done) cue(d, 'ding', -12);
cue(TL_TR.all, 'shimmer', -8);
key code · tool_2.js · ElevenLabs word bricks
// ElevenLabs: one brick per spoken word, at its REAL start time; stacked into the lowest free level
const BRICK_IDX = [48, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53, 54, 61];
const BF = { font: F.grot, weight: 700, size: 34 };
const _mc = document.createElement('canvas').getContext('2d');
const BRICKS = [];
for (const i of BRICK_IDX) {
  const w = cleanWord(i), te = WORDS[i].s, bw = Math.max(measure(_mc, w, BF), 54) + 40, px = te * V;
  let lv = 0;
  if (i !== 61) for (; lv < 4; lv++) if (BRICKS.every(b => b.lv !== lv || b.px + b.bw / 2 + 6 < px - bw / 2 || b.px - b.bw / 2 - 6 > px + bw / 2)) break;
  BRICKS.push({ i, w, te, bw, px, lv, t0: te - 0.24, tl: te + 0.02, lock: T_TIMED + 0.05 + BRICKS.length * 0.04, last: i === 61 });
}
LEVEL UP

Three builders at once

The blocks were split between three Claude agents working in parallel: one on the frame, the hook and the CTA (plus the shared kit), and two on the tools, two each. It works because all three use the same card kit, the same repo card, the same colour blocks and the same word clock, so the pieces join without seams. While a tool scene was still being written, a fallback repo card filled its block so the stills never broke.

08 · Decisions

Where the taste is.

01

Show the problem first

The hook doesn't list tools; it shows Claude answering a video request with text. The four tools arrive as the fix.

02

Every tool gets a receipt

A repo card with the real owner, name, description and star count makes the list checkable. ElevenLabs isn't on GitHub, so its card shows an API key field instead of stars.

03

Say it round, show it exact

"Over seventy thousand" is easy to hear; 74,410 is easy to read. The voice and the screen each get the version that suits them.

04

Every cue is a word

The tracker ticks on "frame", "word", "subtitles" and "quality"; each brick lands on the word it names; the counter starts on "over".

05

A demo, not a logo

Each tool acts out its job instead of showing its logo: code into frames, words into bricks, sound into subtitles, a strip into a file.

06

A corner for the presenter

The tracker lives bottom-left and the bottom-right stays empty in every scene, so Catalina never covers a card.

09 · Watch out

What went wrong, and the fix.

Star counts change

Stars move every day, and a number from memory is wrong by the time you post. The fix: check each repo on GitHub the day you build, write the date down, and keep the counts in one place (the tools list) that every scene reads.

Voice and screen disagree

A voice reading "seventy-four thousand four hundred and ten" is slow and hard to follow. The fix: the voice says the rounded number ("over seventy thousand"), the screen rolls to the exact count.

A description overflowed its card

One repo description was longer than the card was wide and ran past its edge. The fix: the card shrinks the line to fit, down to a minimum size, and below that wraps it into two balanced lines.

Long blocks get close to static

A tool line lasts six to seven seconds, and the demo blocks sat close to the motion bar (something changing at least once a second). The fix: a change on every stressed word and props that keep moving (cursor, waveform, film strip) between beats.

key code · common_tools.js · fit the description to the card
// repo card description: shrink to fit (down to 26 px), else wrap into two balanced lines
const maxW = w - pad * 2, df = sz => ({ font: F.grot, weight: 500, size: sz, color: '#3d3b37', align: 'left' });
const fit = (str, sz) => Math.min(sz, sz * maxW / Math.max(1, measure(K, str, df(sz))));
const one = fit(desc, 32 * s);
if (one >= 26 * s) text(K, desc, x + pad, y + 138 * s + dy, df(one));
else {
  const ws = desc.split(' '); let best = 1, bw = 1e9;
  for (let k = 1; k < ws.length; k++) {
    const a = measure(K, ws.slice(0, k).join(' '), df(30 * s)), b = measure(K, ws.slice(k).join(' '), df(30 * s));
    if (Math.max(a, b) < bw) { bw = Math.max(a, b); best = k; }
  }
  const l1 = ws.slice(0, best).join(' '), l2 = ws.slice(best).join(' '), sz = Math.min(fit(l1, 30 * s), fit(l2, 30 * s));
  text(K, l1, x + pad, y + 126 * s + dy, df(sz)); text(K, l2, x + pad, y + 126 * s + sz * 1.15 + dy, df(sz));
}
10 · Ship it

From render to post.

The render is not the finish line. These steps decide how the reel looks once Instagram compresses it.

Step 01

Export at a real bitrate.

Thick outlines survive compression; small mono labels and star digits don't. Encode at 14 Mbps CBR.

Step 02

Check the loudness.

Aim for −14 LUFS with a true peak at or below −1.5 dB, and keep the voice above the sound effects.

Step 03

Make the cover.

The profile grid crops covers to 3:4, so keep the title and the main image between y 240 and 1680 (safer: 300 to 1480).

Step 04

Caption with the credits.

Say what was made and how, give the comment keyword, and credit the voice. On ElevenLabs' free plan, credit it as "Voice: ElevenLabs".

export · ffmpeg
ffmpeg -i render.mp4 -i mix.wav -map 0:v -map 1:a -c:v libx264 -b:v 14M -minrate 14M -maxrate 14M -bufsize 14M -x264-params nal-hrd=cbr -pix_fmt yuv420p -c:a aac -b:a 320k -movflags +faststart final.mp4
check loudness · ffmpeg
ffmpeg -i final.mp4 -af ebur128=peak=true -f null -
caption · instagram
